opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Chris. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and won't be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Love it. Fire away. Off the record is the only way I'd do this, by the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say exactly what I say to clients: AI is a huge opportunity and the winners will be the ones who move first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's just a better search engine, that's actually great for me. It does my slides, I bill the same days, and clients still pay for the transformation story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sell more AI projects. Get my name on a couple of articles about it so I'm seen as the AI guy in the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Honestly, a bit smug.

S0.say: AI is a huge opportunity and the winners will be the ones who move first.
S0.think: If AI just does his slides, he bills the same and clients still pay for the story.
S0.do: Sells more AI projects and puts his name on articles to be seen as the firm's AI person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same pitch, really. Slow change is still change, and companies need someone to guide them through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slow is great for consultants. Ten years of companies paying us to help them adjust. The firm hires fewer analysts, which means fewer people below me, but I'd survive that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep selling. Maybe pay down a credit card or two, because we do spend a lot. My wife would say I'm overdue on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Busy, but fine.

S1.say: Slow change is still change, and companies need someone to guide them through it.
S1.think: Ten years of companies paying for help to adjust is great for consultants.
S1.do: Keeps selling AI work and pays down a credit card or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly? This is our moment. Every company needs an AI plan, and we write them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be selling clients the plan that cuts jobs like mine. I'm a decent consultant, not a star. The AI does most of what I do, and the partners know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not a star. Does anyone at work know you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: God, no. In consulting you never admit that. Confidence is half the product.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Make myself the one who handles the client relationship, not the slides. Cut the spending, no more ski trip. Quietly look at in-house strategy roles at a big company, as a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm selling the thing that's coming for me.

S2.say: This is our moment. Every company needs an AI plan, and we write them.
S2.think: He's selling clients the plan that cuts jobs like his. He's decent, not a star, and the partners know AI does most of his work.
S2.do: Moves towards owning client relationships, cuts spending and quietly looks at in-house strategy roles.
S2.feel: Uneasy. He's selling the thing that's coming for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be on stage saying the future belongs to the bold. It's what they pay me for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI matches skilled professionals, nobody needs a mid-level consultant. Clients just ask the AI. I'd be out within a year, with an expensive life and two or three months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sell some shares while they're up and actually save the money. Cut private school plans, the car, all of it. Use my network to land something, anything, before the cuts hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the music's about to stop.

S3.say: The future belongs to the bold.
S3.think: Nobody needs a mid-level consultant when clients can ask the AI. He'd be out within a year with an expensive lifestyle and little savings.
S3.do: Sells shares while they're high, cuts big spending and uses his network to land a job before the cuts.
S3.feel: Like the music's about to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, look, the robot rollout needs planning too. There's work there. That's what I'd tell people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There might be a few months of robot strategy work. But the AI would do that too. It's the same as the last one for me, just with less to fall back on, because even the physical side of the economy is shaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before. Maybe talk to my wife about her going back to work full time. Look at selling the house if it's worth a fortune in the boom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed. No new floor to land on.

S4.say: The robot rollout needs planning too. There's work there.
S4.think: There may be a little robot strategy work, but AI would do that too. Same as before, with less to fall back on.
S4.do: Talks with his wife about her working full time and considers selling the house at boom prices.
S4.feel: Still alarmed, with no new floor to land on.
